summary: Verses from four stanzas of the alphabetic psalm of the Torah: the blameless way, a prayer for insight, a vow to keep it.

context.title: The way of God’s teaching
paragraphs: Psalm 119 is an alphabetic poem of twenty-two stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, and every verse of a stanza begins with that letter. [c1] By the count of Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, only two verses lack a word for God’s teaching, which is named by near-synonyms such as law, precepts, judgments and commandments. [c2] The design may have served memory and the instruction of the young. [c3]

Today’s response takes single verses from four stanzas: Aleph, Daleth, He and Vav. [c4] Three of them speak of the way: the blameless way, the way of the precepts and the way of faithfulness. [c5] The psalmist asks for insight, a prayer the psalm repeats, and calls the commandments his delight. [c6][c7]

Verse 44 closes the selection with a vow to keep God’s teaching continually, for ever and ever. [c8] The Cambridge Bible asks whether the singer means only the rest of his own life, or merges himself with the nation and looks to the generations to come. [c8]

translationNotes.summary: Tamim means whole or complete: integrity of life more than spotless purity.
translationNotes.body: Tamim properly means perfect or sincere, a life that is whole, and Barnes compares the description of Job. [c9] The Cambridge Bible explains it as single-hearted devotion to God joined to integrity in dealing with other people. [c10] The older English rendering undefiled matches the Greek and Latin translations, which speak of freedom from stain. [c11]

translationNotes.summary: Piqqudim are things appointed, charges given by God; the word is found only in the Psalms.
translationNotes.body: Piqqud comes from paqad and properly means something appointed, a mandate; it occurs only in the plural. [c12] All twenty-four occurrences are in the Psalms, twenty-one of them in this psalm. [c13] To understand the way of the precepts can mean grasping their full meaning, or learning how to walk by them in daily life. [c14]

translationNotes.summary: A causative verb, “make me understand”, and a request the psalm makes again and again.
translationNotes.body: Havineni is a causative form of bin, to discern: make me understand. [c15] The same verb stands in verse 27, and the request occurs six times in the psalm. [c15][c16] Barnes notes that the psalmist asks not for intelligence in general but for right views of the law. [c17] The Pulpit Commentary paraphrases: if I fail, it is from lack of wisdom, not of will. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: Torah means instruction or teaching before it means a legal code.
translationNotes.body: Torah has a much wider range than law: direction or instruction, human or divine, as when Prov 1:8 speaks of a mother’s torah. [c19] In this psalm it takes in all divine revelation as the guide of life. [c20] Keil and Delitzsch call it living instruction rather than a rigid, fixed teaching. [c21] Rendered simply as law, it can sound like a legal code alone. [c19]

claims.text: Psalm 119 is divided into twenty-two stanzas named by the letters of the Hebrew alphabet; each stanza has eight verses, each beginning with that letter.

By the count of Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, only two verses of Psalm 119 (122 and 132) contain no term for God’s word, which is called by many names such as law, statutes, precepts, judgments and commandments.
Psalm 119 seems intended as a manual of pious thoughts, especially for instructing the young, with a structure that aids memory.
The verses of the responsorial psalm come from four stanzas: Aleph (v. 1), Daleth (vv. 27, 30), He (vv. 34, 35) and Vav (v. 44).
The word דֶּרֶךְ (way) occurs in Psalm 119:1, 27 and 30.
The prayer for deeper insight in Psalm 119:27 recurs in 119:34 and elsewhere in the psalm.
In Psalm 119:35 the psalmist says he delights in the path of God’s commandments.

Psalm 119:44 vows to keep God’s law continually, for ever and ever; the Cambridge Bible asks whether the psalmist means his own lifetime or merges his personality in the nation and its generations to come.
תָּמִים properly means perfect or sincere, and Barnes compares the word used of Job in Job 1:1.
The perfect in way are those whose course of life is governed by single-hearted devotion to God and integrity in dealing with others.
The Greek translation of Psalm 119:1 renders the word undefiled, and the Latin immaculati.
פִּקּוּד comes from פָּקַד and properly means a thing appointed, a mandate; it is used only in the plural.
פִּקּוּד occurs twenty-four times, all in the Psalms, twenty-one of them in Psalm 119.
Understanding the way of the precepts may mean grasping their full meaning or knowing how to walk according to them.
In the petition “give me understanding”, which occurs six times in Psalm 119, the verb is causative.
The verb in Psalm 119:34 is the same as in Psalm 119:27.
Psalm 119:34 is not a prayer for the faculty of intelligence but for right views of the law.
The Pulpit Commentary paraphrases Psalm 119:34 as: if I fail now, it is from lack of wisdom, not of will.
Torah has a much wider range of meaning than law: direction or instruction, human (Prov 1:8) or divine, a body of teaching, a code, the Pentateuch.
In Psalm 119, as in Psalms 1 and 19, torah includes all divine revelation as the guide of life.
In Psalm 119 torah has not the rigid notion of a fixed teaching but of living instruction.
